utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecutor, along with Mr. Huber, who has just stepped out for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We also have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Niko Duric, attorney at law from Zagreb, Croatia representing Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. Mr. Delic is also represented by Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey, from the United States, and I represent Mr. Esad Landzo, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, also from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we are ready for Mr. Moran's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, may it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. Ustalic, would you please state your full name for the record so that the Court reporter can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a minute, please. Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if the witness could turn on his microphone. Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. THE COURT: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ustalic, would you please state your full name for the record so the Court reporter can take it down.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: My name is Zlatko Ustalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ustalic, how are you employed now?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I work for the Igman Company, which is part of the UNIS conglomerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What do you do for them, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I do jobs that are required of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, during the war, and I want you to focus on -- yes, sir, what jobs are required of you? What are your basic duties for the Igman Company?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: You mean at the job on which I work? It is maintenance of machinery. We are repairing things that have been damaged in the war. We are trying to make them up and running so that we could go on producing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And are you married man, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, I am married and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was my next question, you anticipated me, sir. I sir, I would like to focus your attention on the war, and mainly the period from May through December of 1992. What did you do during the war, during that period of the war?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I was assigned to duties as a driver who was distributing food along the front lines to the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Tell the judges, just in general, what your duties were when you say you distributed food along the frontlines to the fighters. For instance, did you pick the -- did you get the food at some central location and take it out, and, if so, how did you do it? Just in general terms, so the judges can know your general duties.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Around 20 April a mobilisation took place and commander at that time, Esad Ramic, assigned me to be driver with a quarter master's office. I had a Lada vehicle, which I used to distribute the food at the front lines, where necessary, but this was an old car, so we had to look after spare parts. There was a lot of shelling. We could not move about freely. We were limited in terms of picking up the food that was prepared at Igman Company. And later on it was prepared at the Cipad factory. It was the food that was prepared for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't want to lead you, and I don't want to suggest to you what you should say, but did you get these things in, what, great big pots and put them in the back of your vehicle and then just move them, take them to various places?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I was only a driver. I only drove. I had a colleague who did this. His name was Mirsad Landzo. He would take the food, he would load it up into the vehicle, and then it would be taken to its destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you -- by the way, when you say Mirsad Landzo, do you know if he is any relation to Esad Landzo who is sitting over there? If you don't know, you don't know, but just out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: When I entered the Courtroom, I recognised Mucic and Mr. Delalic and Mr. Delic, but I could not recognise Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Sir, were part of your duties to take food to the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did that include food for both the staff and the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: At first it was only for the personnel, for the staff, and later on it was also for the prisoners, after the prisoners had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That was -- do you remember about when you started bringing food for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Sometime in May. Maybe mid-may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I'm sure you didn't write it down, don't have any specific memory, and that's fine. Sir, tell the judges how you actually delivered the food to the barracks, and there's a model behind you if you want to -- if it would help to you show the judges -- if you want to use the model, that's just fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose his first answer was he was only a driver. There was someone else who would load the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To do the delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This Mr. Landzo that helped you load the van, did he go with you when you were delivering the food?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when you drove up to the Celebici barracks to deliver food, basically, what did you do and how did you deliver it?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: At the gate there was a guard. He would open the gate. We would arrive, we would make a left turn, we would arrive in front of the administration building. And there the food would be unloaded and I think Sejvudin Sok would take it over there for the staff before the prisoners arrived, and after the prisoners had arrived, Sejvudin also took -- would take the food, and there were also two girls. I think there was one name was Meliha, something like that. And later on the prisoners themselves would take over the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you see the prisoners take the food back to the hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No. I don't know about hangar number 6. I don't know what that is. But I would arrive at the administration building. I could show it to you on the model and that's where I would be -- can I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: (Witness indicating) The food would be delivered at this location here, and after unloading the food I would go this way and I would come to the hangar and I would give the food to the weapons people. There were three weapons, technicians there. I can't recall their names. And then I would go back and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, the food for the prisoners, was that a small quantity of food or a large quantity of food, or was it the same amount, roughly, per person -- well, that the fighters were getting, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Let me just repeat it again. I was only a driver and a colleague who was with me, and I saw this because I could not not see it. For instance, people at the front lines and people at different points, they all received the same food, and it would be about one quarter a loaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One quarter loaf of bread?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: For both the prisoners and the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many prisoners there were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but at least 70 breads would be brought in, so multiplied by four, so let's say 280.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How often did you bring in the breads and the rest of the food? Once a day, twice a day, three times a day? Every other day? How often, roughly?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Breakfast, lunch and dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And after you delivered the food, for instance at a lunch, would you stay at the Celebici barracks or would you go someplace else and then return? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I had several drop-off points, something like 15. One was Podgradac, Loncari, the school, Celebici, Ostrozac, Turija. I could not stay around for a long time. You can understand. And it's breakfast, lunch and dinner. It was a lot of food to be distributed around. Did I not have time to linger around much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then after you continued on your rounds, would you come back and pick up empty pots and empty -- and take them back to the central kitchen, so that they could be reused?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: In the beginning, when the prisoners would not receive their meals, the breakfast went on very quickly, we didn't have to stay long. When the prisoners arrived, the military had spare mess tins and we would give them these extras, and we would pick up the other ones. So it wouldn't stay a long time. And then we -- sometimes we did not have enough of the large containers because I had to take them all the way out to Klise (Phon) and other locations. So we would then substitute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you often bring them cooked food besides just the bread?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. For breakfast, there was tea, coffee with milk, and some eggs. Sometimes for a while there was even some honey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how about lunch, what would they get for lunch? What would you bring to the camp?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Lentils, beans, stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And dinner would be the same as lunch, basically?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the amount of food you were bringing to the people in the camp, the number of prisoners, was it about the same amount of food as you were getting, when you consider how many prisoners you estimate were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I did not fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. And it was a poorly phrased question. It was my fault, not yours. You estimated -- you said you brought about 70 loaves of bread for the prisoners, and everybody got a quarter of a loaf, so you were guessing about 280 people, give or take a few, that were prisoners. When you consider the amount of food that you brought for the prisoners at the camp, and you figure there was about 280 people are going to be eating this amount of food, was it about the same amount of food as you were getting? Each person's portion would be about the same as yours?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were there, sir, did you ever see Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: You mean Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: He would be at the gate, sometimes at the reception, and for the rest was doing whatever the other guards were around there were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him give any orders to anyone, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I did not have many opportunities, and we didn't stay around much, very long. So I did not have many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did -- when you were there, did you get very close to the prisoners that were being held in the camp? Could you see them closely and observe them closely?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I could not approach them, but I could see the people who were taking the food away to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And those people that you saw, those prisoners that were carrying the food to the other prisoners, or, for that matter, any of the prisoners, any of them look like they had been beaten up or starved or kicked, or hit, or burned up or abused in any way?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: My colleague from work, his name was Vukasin Mrkajic. We used to work for the same company. He would take the food and would carry it over to the prisoners. I could not notice any changes in him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did he look like he had lost weight, or --

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I believe that I was thinner than he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get to talk to Mr. Mrkajic when he was there?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I was not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Zdravko Mucic also has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The Defence of Esad Landzo does have some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination by the Prosecution, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll state for the Court and for the witness that I've had a cold and a cough for the last few days so I'll just have my water handy there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ustalic, my name is Nancy Boler and along with Cynthia McMurrey I represent Esad Landzo. You and I have met before, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And we first met in May, when I came to Konjic, and then again briefly when I was there two weeks ago, right?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And when you and I spoke briefly a couple of weeks ago, you told me that your mother was afraid for to you come and testify, right?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: My apologies. I forgot this. But, thank you for reminding me. Your Honours, if I am free to say this. I am in -- offended that I have received this subpoena. I never said that I would not come here to say the truth, so that the whole truth be told here. I requested that -- including the lady here, because my mother is sick, I asked Mr. Karabdic and also Madam -- oh, sorry, neither madam Nancy did this or Mr. Karabdic didn't do that. So I don't feel good about being brought here in this manner. I wanted to come, but I wanted to come here to speak the truth. And I am glad that the truth is going to come out of this. And thank you for reminding me, so that I can make this comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And when I was there, I explained to you that Mr. Delic would probably be bringing you here by subpoena, and in fact, you are here by subpoena today, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You don't really have to ask him that. We know he's here on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You have previously spoken to representatives of the Defence of Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, I had separate meetings with the gentleman for Mr. Landzo and with a different gentleman for Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: In fact, December 26th of 1992 you gave a statement to Mrs. Brackovic, who is the wife of Mr. Landzo's original attorney; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You said 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I meant to say 1992, what did I say? I meant to say 1996. Did I say 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay, sorry. It was 1996. Do you remember giving that statement to Mrs. Brackovic.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You'll see a lot of these questions I am crossing out because Mr. Moran asked you the same questions. We understand that you were a driver during the war and you mentioned that there was a great deal of shelling at that time, in fact, your own vehicle was fired upon by the Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and that was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And this type of activity caused a lot of fear amongst the people in Konjic, did it not?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm also going to ask you a few questions about delivering the food to Celebici, as Mr. Moran did. Mr. Moran asked you about your partner, I suppose we'll call him, Mr. Mirsad Landzo. And Mr. Landzo was a cousin of Esad Landzo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: You said my colleague. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Close enough. I said partner, but colleague means the same thing. You mentioned it in direct, that a gentleman named Mr. Mirsad Landzo accompanied you or was also part of the food delivery service, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: That is correct. Mirsad Landzo was with me throughout this time, and we drove the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And he was seriously injured during the war, in fact, his left arm is still disabled; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Also, when you were speaking with -- answering Mr. Moran's questions, you mentioned that you did not recognise Mr. Landzo this morning. But you knew him during the war, did you not?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I could not see him, and right now I can't see him in the Courtroom. I see the other gentlemen, but I can't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what he said, on coming in he recognised Delalic, Mucic and Delic. He did not know the other person. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if it was because of the pillar was in the way, if he saw him, but did not recognise him, that that was Mr. Landzo, or if there was an obstruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you now see Mr. Landzo in the Courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And he doesn't look malnourished anymore, he has grown from a boy into a man, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I just notice him. I saw a figure back there. He doesn't look as the boy which I used to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, when Mr. Moran was asking you about the food, you mentioned some of these foods, but let me just reiterate that you -- when you made these deliveries, that the food consisted mainly of beans, rice, macaroni, lentil soup and such; is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And also when canned meat was available, a 400 gram tin of meat was shared between two and four prisoners, right?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did you stay approximately one half hour at Celebici when you made your deliveries?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I didn't have that much time to stay there, because I had to go to other drop-off points. I repeat again, I said that I had a very bad car, that I had to take care of the oil, the wheels and everything else, the situation was very bad, and therefore, I would like to repeat again that you must understand that I had a very difficult job. I had a lot of things to do, which I -- which I did not have enough time. And I had to get up very early and at the evening when I would come home, I would realise that I had no time to eat because I was surrounded by the smell of food all day long.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Thank you for expanding on your answer. During the time that you were in Celebici, when you made your deliveries, did you observe that small groups of prisoners would put food on their own plates; in other words, the prisoners -- you observed the prisoners distributing the food themselves, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I couldn't see that. I would only see that the prisoners would take -- were taking the food away from the command building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My next question would be, then, the guards did not decide which prisoners got what amounts of food in your observance, did they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you ask him such questions? He's told you he never spent any time there. He was in a hurry and he left almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard him say that he observed the prisoners taking the food away, so that was just a follow-up question, since he testified that he observed the prisoners taking the food away. I just followed up. Maybe I should rephrase it and say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You never saw the camp guards taking that food away? It's your testimony that you saw the prisoners taking the food away, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: They would take their food, the food which was meant for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Now, when you brought the food to Celebici, did Mr. Delic sign receipts for the amount of food that you brought?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: At sometimes, yes, of course, but whoever wanted to from the guards could sign these receipts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you kept the receipts, right?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No. Both me and my colleagues could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. I guess my point of my question is, if we had those receipts today, then the Trial Chamber would be able to know exactly how much food was delivered, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean for the period, the whole period -- the period when he delivered?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My understanding he said he delivered -- let me ask you this question, Mr. Ustalic, since the judge brought this up. My understanding is that you delivered food from mid-April of 1992 until the end of the year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And during that time period, if we had those receipts today, would the Trial Chamber be able to see exactly how many food was delivered to Celebici? Was that information on those receipts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him. Ask him what did he do with those receipts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ustalic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe he deposited them at the place where he got the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: After you got the receipts back from Mr. Delic or whoever signed for the receipts, what did you do with the receipts?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Those were not receipts. It was a block which came from the kitchen of Igman and Cipad. That means, for example, if you took five loaves of bread, this receipt would say Ustalic and Landzo took five loaves of bread. And that means that somebody else had to sign this receipt that this was taken, because I had to show this to my superior that this job was done. Because a soldier cannot survive without food. And let me answer the question of the judge. This -- these receipts existed. I would give them to Mr. Nehir, and I think that he would copy some of them, he would copy some of them, and I kept those. I had them. And I kept it in my cellar, but since I had a flood in my cellar, there was a catastrophe. But I'm really sorry about that. I really did keep records of everything that I took, even toothpicks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And when you say that you gave the receipts to Mr. Nehir, do you mean the investigator for Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on. During the -- and I understand to you say that it was short times that you were in Celebici when you delivered the food. Did you also -- you observed the families of detainees bringing food, shoes, clothing, et cetera, to their relatives, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: The families of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I didn't see the families, but how should I put this? There were more families, men and women, children, the elderly, who would carry things in bags. I don't know what they were carrying, but I would see that this was being received at the gate. I would see that this commotion, that some things were being given, but I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did you say you saw the guards take these things from the families?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Well, I remember one man, because this man is now my neighbour. His name is Muharem Masic. And he would take these gifts and he would give them to the prisoners. He would give these things to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And you observed that when you were there? I'll retract that. Obviously, that's what you just stated. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Could I say something else? When I was passing with my car, this would be at the gate on the left for me. There was a larger line, which was waiting, a longer line, and they were holding bags in their hand and there were children and women and the elderly. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And also when you were there, you observed the prisoners engaging in other activities, such as bathing, correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Once I could see, when I went to see Nurko, Nurko Tabak, who was the weapons specialist, they were having showers. They were using a fire-fighting hose, and from afar I could see that they were taking showers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a couple of more questions about Mr. Landzo, and then I will wind up. Starting in mid-July of 1992, you saw that Esad Landzo was a guard at the prison, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He hasn't said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And you never observed Mr. Landzo distribute any food to the prisoners; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Microphone, please, Your Honour) he didn't say any such thing.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, I never observed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Isn't it also true that for a certain period of time the prisoners -- the prisoners at Celebici were actually given better food than the soldiers on the front line, but that that was something you all kept quiet, so as not to cause dissatisfaction among the soldiers; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have asked three questions in one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That's probably why he doesn't understand the question. Let me break it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that during certain periods of time the prisoners at Celebici were actually given better food to eat than your soldiers on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: If on the better food you would consider a can, a so-called duck, which had 400 grams, and a soldier would receive cooked food, then, because meat is meat and soup is a soup.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let my final question be -- I'll ask you to describe how Mr. Landzo today looks different from the way he looked back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Well, I would like Esad Landzo to stand up so that I can see him. But I can describe him, what he looked like. He was a very thin boy, had short hair. He had a large uniform on, large -- the sleeves were large. He had a big rifle and the butt was touching the ground. The rifle seemed to be larger than him because he didn't seem to weigh more than 30 kilos and he would open the gate for me, when I would pass through the gate. That's when I would see him, and not on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ustalic, thank you for coming to the Hague to testify. I pass the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, my name is Teresa McHenry and I have some questions for you. If you don't understand my question, please tell me and I will rephrase it or repeat it. Okay?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For how long a period of time did you deliver food to the Celebici prison? I know you started, you believe, sometime in May. How long did you deliver, did you continue to deliver food there?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: You mean the exact date when I stopped delivering food?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The approximate date. The month even.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Sometime in October '92. After that I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who -- do you know who took over for you when you left in October of '92? Did someone else take over the job of driving food to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do. It was my colleague, Mirsad Landzo. He continued. And Muharem Slato. He continued with the distribution. He was a driver for another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mucic was the commander of the Celebici prison for most of the time you were driving there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this question. It's leading. He didn't say that. He just said that he recognised my client here in the Courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Cross-examination can lead. It doesn't stop a cross examiner leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Mucic was the commander of the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I was not in the position to know such things. I don't know if he was a commander. During my time there, I saw him in mid-August, maybe, and then at the end of August, at most. Maybe twice at most that I -- it was twice that I saw him at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that at the time you believed that Mr. Mucic was the commander, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has told you he could not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: I object again to this line of questioning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask more specifically, sir. You've talked about giving statements to the Defence before, and in particular talking with a Mr. Nehir. Let me ask you if you remember stating in a prior statement, and if you -- I'll ask the usher to give you a copy of it. Do you remember stating, "From the time I started delivering food, that is, from the time the Celebici barracks was first established, the barracks commander was Dzevad Alibasic and later Zdravko Mucic. I do not recall the exact date when the post was passed from one to the other, but I know that Alibasic was the commander for a very brief period before Pavo Mucic took over his post." Do you remember -- may I ask that the witness be shown his prior statement. Sir, do you remember saying that previously?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I cannot remember if this is true. I don't think I wrote this. I think the attorney wrote this. Please, I came here to tell the truth and nothing but the truth and don't lead me to tell lies, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask that you look at the last page of that, sir, and ask -- the last page of it, which is the Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I signed this. This is my signature. But this gentleman wrote what he wanted to. And you didn't see correctly. It says here that for this -- it should say that for this statement I will be responsible in front of the Tribunal at the Hague, but it's not stated here. It was left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It does say, sir, right before your signature, "That none of the statements I have made here was given under duress in any way, and I hereby recognise and sign as my own concerning what I saw and what I know about the events and situation in the Celebici barracks." That's what it says right above your signature, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: This is not mine. This was added by the attorney who wrote this. This was his wish. And please do not force me to lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir. When you gave this statement and signed it and said that it was true, were you being forced to lie at that time?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No. At the beginning they were talking. I said earlier that I was very upset because I came under a subpoena. They promised that another version, they said that they would be connected through satellites, that we would be in Sarajevo, and that we could do this through a satellite. And this is not my statement. This is what the attorney wrote. And I will only be speaking the truth, and that is why I came here for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question, sir, then is: Why, if what's in here is not the truth, did you say, "I recognise and sign as my own all statements concerning what I saw and what I know". If what is in this statement isn't true, sir, why did you sign it and say that it was true?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I would like to repeat once again, this is not mine. This was done quickly and this is not my statement. This is not my personal statement. This is what the lawyer wrote. Because he made us work things very quickly, and he did it at his own will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my -- you've already indicated -- well, let me just repeat. You would agree with me that you signed this statement in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think you should move to something else, because he signed this statement, he is now denying it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will move on. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did you get -- did you -- well, let me just ask you, sir. You would agree, wouldn't you, that when you went to Celebici, it was usually to Mr. Delic that you delivered the food, and it was Mr. Delic who would tell you how many prisoners there were, so you would know how much food to bring the next time? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: When Hazim Delic happened to be there, he could give the -- any prisoner could give the number of -- any guard -- interpreter correction -- any guard could give the number of prisoners and it was my colleague who would take this number. I wouldn't be responsible for this. And it was the kitchen that would establish how much food was necessary to bring to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sometimes, when you went to the prison, it was to Mr. Delic, you were present when Mr. Delic talked about how much food -- how many prisoners there were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, sir, that Mr. Delic is the person who would often give the number of prisoners to you or to your colleague?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so if your statement says that, that would be another thing that's incorrect in your statement?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I would like again to repeat that the attorney himself wrote this statement. These are not my words. I was present when this was being written, but these are not my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt. I would like this statement to be withdrawn, because he denied it and the question should be -- should not be based on this statement at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, you don't withdraw a statement because he denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: But further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He made the statement, he signed it, but he's denied the contents. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I agree with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Someone else had put in things which he did not tell him. This is what he is saying. You don't, because of that, withdraw a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that, but I was not going in that direction. Actually, Ms. McHenry keeps asking the question on the basis of the statement that this witness had denied. So I would like, you know, to clarify this -- that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think I agree with you. Counsel is merely pointing out facts in a statement which he said he did not make. This is all she was doing. He said certain things and he signed it after making this statement. But he now says he did not say those things. So this is what she is trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. Delic have any role with respect to logistics in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in part he delivered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is the other man going along with him, Mirsad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But he stated he was often present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if Mr. Delic had any -- was in charge of logistics in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Tell him what logistics is. Does he know? It's a technical term. Ask him, does he understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, ask him pointedly whether he said so in his statement. If he did not say so, and this also was inserted by the attorney, then you know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what logistics is?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes. I was a logistics person. I worked in the logistics group. And logistics takes care about the medical care, food distribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that Hazim Delic was in charge of logistics at Celebici camp, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you remember whether or not you indicated to the investigator that Hazim Delic was in charge of logistic matters?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because when this gentleman asked us to say what he wanted to hear, and to have written down with respect to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So the investigator would tell you what he wanted to hear, and you would then repeat it to him, and he would write it down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No. He was writing -- he wrote this already and then he read it aloud to us and he said, "This is what it's going to be like."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, sir. If I understood you correctly, you just stated that you did tell the investigator that Mr. Delic was in charge of logistics; is that correct, that you told the investigator that Mr. Delic was in charge of logistics?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, I did not say that he was in charge of logistics. But Mr. Delic often gave the number of prisoners and took care of the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, my question to you just a minute ago, sir, was did you indicate to the investigator that Mr. Delic was in charge of logistics, and you said, "Yes, I did." Do you remember saying that a couple of minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, can you please -- you discussed this briefly with Mr. Moran, but I didn't really understand it all. Can you please explain to us when you would bring the food to Celebici, what you could see of the kind of containers it was in? And I am talking about both breakfast and lunch and dinner. Can you just explain that to me in a little more detail what you remember about it?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I don't know what you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am interested in the size of the containers, what kind of containers there were, whether or not you gave them utensils, how you brought coffee and tea. I am interested in all those kinds of details.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, as -- let me repeat it. I was a driver. I drove the vehicle and my colleague was distributing food. I know what these containers were. They were larger size --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just maybe with your hands indicate approximately sort of how big they were, just approximately, for the food.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And if you remember, approximately how many of those would you bring?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: What do you mean? To the prison or the front lines? Oh, Celebici. There was one large container, one smaller container. So two containers, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And I am assuming that the one you just showed us the approximate dimensions of was the large container. Can you give us just -- show us with your hands again the approximate dimensions of the smaller container.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: (Witness indicating) Like this. Not much smaller, but smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And would you drop both -- when you came in and went to the administration building, would both those containers be brought -- taken off the truck or the car at the administration building?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Mirsad Landzo would drop off one set and pick up another set. We had to move on, to go to the next point. We would just drop off one set and we would pick up the other ones, to take it back to the central kitchen, so that there would be washed. We had to do it constantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Tell me if I understand you correctly, sir. You would come in, you would go to the administration building, and you would unload these two containers and then you would leave?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No madam. We would arrive at the administration building, Mirsad Landzo would unload these two containers. He would load up the two empty ones, and we would go on, on our way. And this is the procedure that we followed throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when is it that you would go to the weapons -- the weapons people? After you dropped off the food at the administration building?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And so what would -- where would they get their food, if the containers were already at the administration building? What is it that you would give to the people in the weapons warehouse?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, we had another point, Celebici and Orahovica and Ostrozac and below Ostrozac there was another one, I can't recall. So there was additional food. So people who had their own containers, we would -- he would put -- ladle out the food into their plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you could see, after you dropped the food off, you could see the prisoners come and get the food from the big containers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Did I see the prisoners taking the food away? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, could you see the prisoners taking the food away from the command -- the administration building, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, as far as I could see from the administration building to the infirmary across the street, that is as far as I could see. Not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But if I understood you correctly, in direct testimony you indicated that you could see the prisoners take the food away from the area of the administration building? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, madam, you understood my correctly. And I had repeated that. Because the administration building and the infirmary were one across from the other, and that was my field of vision. Maybe that's about 20 or 30 metres where they were taking the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you correctly, you saw prisoners taking the food to the infirmary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Towards the infirmary, madam. If I understand, the administration building is on one side and the infirmary was on the other. And so they were going down that street on which I was not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just on the model show us the street that you were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I just showed it a moment ago. This is where I would deliver the food. So this would be the infirmary. And I couldn't even go as far as this point. This was where I would park. So I couldn't see beyond this. So they would take it from here and they would take the food -- then we would then go to Nurko over this way, drop off food there, and then go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you go back the same way, in other words, you are saying you would never make a circle around the camp, you would go by the tunnel and then back again?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, could you just again show me one more time the route that you would take when you went to deliver the food to the weapons people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The route he took on his way back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I would enter at the gate. I would bring the food to the administration building. This is where the food would be taken for the prisoner, and then I would go this way and come to Nurko's workshop, and then I would return that way back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And how did you know that you weren't allowed to go on that other street? Did someone tell that you, that you weren't allowed to go in that direction?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, there was a barrier there. I could not pass there. There was a fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you show us where on the model the fence was, and tell us what kind of fence it was.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Here it was (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let the record reflect the witness marked right in front of Witness D, a fence around -- and did it prevent any vehicles from going, from passing, was it large enough to prevent vehicles from passing through on the street?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: It was simple fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it a metal fence or a wooden fence?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, metal, yes. It was just like a wire and it was stretched both ends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was it there the entire time that you delivered food to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I would notice it always. I knew from day one when the prisoners arrived there that I was not allowed to move there. So I did not after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did the fence have a door on it? Was there a way that if the people in the prison wanted to open the street, so that vehicles could pass through, that they could do so?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, it was just simple wire, which was at maybe 30, 40 centimetres height, that is when I was -- when I first saw it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if someone wanted, they could have removed the wire; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you indicated that you could see the prisoners take the food in some direction, would they take the big pots that you've talked about, or would they have smaller containers? And if they had smaller containers, can you please again, with just -- just indicate about how big they were.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I told you there was one large container, one smaller container, one had already been prepared, which we would pick up, load into the vehicle. We would give them the full one, the full container of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And my question is, sir, you indicated that you could see prisoners take the food away from the command centre, away from the command building?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And my question is: In what container were the prisoners taking the food away in?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: In the containers which I have already mentioned, which we had brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would the prisoners, on the occasions when you saw them, would they be taking both containers with them or just one of the containers?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I would see four men, they would carry the containers, and one of them would have to come back for bread, for the loaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, then what would the guards eat, if the prisoners took both containers that you brought to Celebici? What did the guards eat?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I said that there was a separate container for the guards. It was a smaller one for the guards, for the staff who -- which worked at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you would drop off three containers of food; is that what you are saying now?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: The question, madam, was how much was I delivering for the prisoners, in terms of food. I think that that was the question. And I said that Sefudin in the beginning would take it first and then the two girls, Meliha was one of them, they would take this food and then they would take -- they would carry their food and the others would carry their own food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how many containers would you bring for the guards and the personnel in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: One. One smaller one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was it the same size, approximately, as the smaller one that the prisoners were given, or was it even smaller than that?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Still smaller than theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just please again with your hands indicate, show us about the size of the -- the guards would get.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Like this (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, I assume, since you were told approximately how many prisoners were there, you have some idea of how many personnel there were in the Celebici barracks. About how much -- about how many people worked in the Celebici barracks that you would bring food for? Not the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I don't know that, madam, because the number of them would change. The kitchen would sometimes give food for eight, sometimes for ten. It kept changing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, approximately, how many loaves of bread you would bring for the personnel?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Five. Up to six, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, would you bring utensils for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to see them, and, in fact, madam, I just drove the vehicle and my colleague handled the food. I drove the vehicle and I am just telling you what I could see indirectly. Because I did not pay attention that much. I am just speaking from my memory and I am telling you what I can remember. And I remember that I had troubles with this vehicle because I had troubles with it all the time. I was always weary of whether there would be -- whether the tires would blow or there the oil would run out. So I did not pay that much attention to any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about bringing coffee and tea and eggs. Was that for the prisoners or for the personnel or both?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, it was the same for both, the prisoners. They would receive the same eggs, the same tea, the same coffee. It was the same quantities for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what kind of containers would the coffee and the tea for the prisoners come in?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: In the same containers, except that they were washed, because they were Teflon containers. They were not -- they were not pots. They were airtight, so that -- so they would keep the food warm until it was brought to these points. And eggs we brought in large pots like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And approximately how many -- how often would you bring eggs to the prisoners in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is it the case that you would bring coffee and tea for the prisoners, breakfast, lunch and dinner?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I said that coffee came for breakfast or it was tea, and then with tea or tea or coffee there was eggs or honey, small packages of honey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So the coffee and tea would only be for breakfast and not for lunch and dinner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, madam, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so would the prisoners come, bring the food, and then come back for the coffee and tea for these big containers of coffee and tea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He must have left again by the time the prisoners ate their meal, because he had to go to other locations. How would he know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: They may have done it at the same time or he may have seen it on the way back. If he doesn't know, he can say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know, sir? Did you ever see any prisoner with a container of coffee or tea?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I saw them carrying eggs and coffee or tea. They were carrying it away in front of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would they get either coffee or tea every breakfast?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I am going to object that this line of questioning is irrelevant, besides being asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the prisoners get coffee or tea every day for breakfast?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No they did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And can you estimate how often they would get coffee or tea, or you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many times, but it was frequently that they would receive this type of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, were there some occasions where you couldn't bring food three times a day to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, never. It never happened that we could not bring food every day, but since Konjic was shelled all the time, we would sometimes have to wait until the shelling stopped, because we would wait at the mess hall for several hours. So if there was shelling in the morning, the breakfast would be a bit late, but maybe up to an hour, because we could not leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But you are sure that every day the prisoners -- you delivered food to Celebici three times, three separate times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, ma'am. That is the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you talked about seeing a Mr. Masic, you saw persons at the gate giving items to Mr. Masic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: As I said, ma'am, I did see Mr. Masic, as he was receiving these packages, and I saw groups of people, elderly women and children, to the left as you were entering the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that you never saw the prisoners being given any of those items? I am not saying it didn't happen, but you never saw it, did you?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you talked about these receipts that you would -- well, actually, let me back up. So if I understand you correctly, you would never bring breakfast and lunch at the same time, or lunch and dinner at the same time? It would always be separate because you would go three times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Madam, I had to, because Celebici was just up one point for me. I had another five points beyond Celebici, because soldiers had -- if there was food, he had to receive breakfast, lunch and dinner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sometimes, because you had so many places to go and because of problems, would you deliver lunch and dinner at the same time -- with the same delivery?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, ma'am, it never happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that at least in 1996 you had possession of some receipts. The receipts you had from when you delivered food to Celebici, would you get a receipt every time that you brought food or just some occasions?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Ma'am, I said that this was a logbook -- actually, it was four with receipts and let's say it stated there 100 loaves were issued and 500 meals, and then you had to go to Podgradac, Ostrozac, Loncari, the school, Glavicine, and I had to deliver it to all these points, this food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question was, when you delivered food to Celebici, would someone sign every time you delivered food to indicate receipt of the food?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Of course, that had to be done. Because we had control. Because my superior controlled this. It was my colleagues duties, but if he didn't do it, I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you indicated that at least in 1996 you gave certain receipts to Mr. Nehir. Do you remember approximately how many receipts you gave Mr. Nehir, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Ma'am, I gave it to Mr. Nehir. Mr. Nehir photocopied them and I saw some of these receipts photocopied with him. But what he did with them -- I used to have the originals, as I said, maybe it would have been easier on both of us if I had given -- if I had this to give you, but my basement was flooded, so it was -- it has all perished.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, when you saw that Mr. Nehir had photocopied some receipts, do you have any idea about how many receipts Mr. Nehir had photocopied?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I believe that Ms. Nancy or Christina may be familiar with that. Think that they took it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And did someone recently show you any of those photocopies?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw some photocopies of your receipts?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Before I came here, when I couldn't, when I, and when I asked them to talk to my mother about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you remember, approximately, how many receipts you saw?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I believe three or four, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the witness be shown three documents. We have extra copies. They were received from Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's time for a break and we'll reassemble at 1.00. The Trial Chamber will now reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mrs. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 23, 24 and 25/3. These have previously been shown by Mr. Moran, but they have not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These are the receipts?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise those documents, and if so, can you tell us what they are, please?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I was talking about. And there are other two or three documents, ma'am. But I don't know why the Defence didn't show them. It was kept in a book and this is what they looked like. I don't know why this logbook wasn't shown. I gave this book, which contained the signatures of Mr. Hazim Delic and some other signatures. There are two. And they are not like this. These are in a logbook. But this is also right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you, there were some receipts that were kept separate and there was another logbook that had Mr. Delic's signature and other peoples on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: No, ma'am, that's not correct, because we ran out of these receipts and, therefore, the rest was kept in the logbook. And Mr. Nehir took these away from me, and I don't know why he showed them to you -- why he did not show them to you, these -- this logbook exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you -- have you seen the logbook recently? Do you have any idea where it is now?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I saw it at Mr. Nehir's, as I said earlier, the last time when he spoke to me, and I don't know where it is now, whether it's here or not. But I saw it in his possession when he was in Konjic. Maybe you should ask Mr. Saloh (sic).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is the interpreter going to correct something?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Nehir is an investigator who works for Mr. Karabdic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: That's what he said to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just ask that you sort of now look at this document, and let me start, please, with the document dated the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt for a very brief moment, Your Honours. These translations are a little bit deficient, because according to the original photocopy, which I believe these are, in the second column there is the word -- an abbreviation, KOM, which in Croatian means peace. This particular indication does not appear in the English translation. This is left vacant. On the column which is titled "measure" there is a blank space. It should be filled with the proper translation which appears in the Croatian document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: These were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any other observation, make them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, referring to the document dated the 15th of June, which is D24/3. Can you tell me whose signature appears on those -- on it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: This is my signature here on the right-hand side, and the goods which were taken from the warehouse, Almir Musinovic. This is how I took the goods from the warehouse, and it was then loaded into the car and taken further. That's why I am telling you that there was another logbook, and I -- it's really strange, ma'am, that these documents are not here, because I gave them to Nehir to copy them. And it's really strange that you don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I wish I had them too, sir. So would anybody on this kind of receipt, would anybody from -- at the prison sign this document, or is it only you and the person at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: The person who issued -- the person issued this -- these goods at the warehouse, and I took them, and then these goods were taken further to the point of distribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when you -- would you bring this bill -- this receipt to Celebici and would someone from Celebici sign it, or is that separate? That's this logbook that you were telling about that you gave to Mr. Nehir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think counsel is suggesting, when you brought it to the Celebici barracks and somebody received it from you, did that person sign it?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so on this document, D24, does the signature of anyone from Celebici appear?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Naturally, ma'am, what I gave to Mr. Nehir contains all of that, who gave the goods, who received the goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So it's not -- it would not be on this receipt, it would be on this other logbook that you gave to Mr. Nehir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct. This is a receipt that I took from -- that I took from the warehouse, this and the other one, and the third one also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you look at this, it says fully transferred and dispatched by Turin (Phon). This time when he signed for it. It's not likely to be the one he delivered to some other group at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if you look at the original, which the English is, the following items were dispatched, is part of a form, either by train, post, crate or package, and it appears that none of them are indicated. And this witness has said these are -- reflects the goods that he received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, sir, am I correct that on this form you wouldn't -- would not fill out, that you were taking these items by car? Sir, if you look at the document, is that just part of the form that you would not fill out, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: I only signed this, ma'am, that I received the goods, and then I dispatched it further, because the goods could not go anywhere without that. And this was under the control of Mr. Mirsad Ramic, and the person who worked in the warehouse, Mr. Almir, was responsible for the goods and me and Mr. Landzo would just distribute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you look at this, it shows that the person who issued it to him, and he is receiving it. These are the only signatures which are here. Not the person who received it from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's what he said. My question had to be I wasn't sure what was this signature under which where it says Ustalic. That was my question. But he's answered it and Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this book by -- that you gave Mr. Nehir, and you've indicated that it is your own book, would it be acceptable for you if I looked at that book? In other words, sir, if it's your book, you could ask -- I am wondering whether or not you would agree that I can ask Mr. Karabdic to show me your book, since he's now in possession of it, or his defence. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would call on Mr. Karabdic to make available to me now or in the near future a copy of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has he got it in his possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The investigator received this logbook, this is what I was informed, and from this book he copied only those parts where he could find the signature of Hazim Delic, and after that he returned this book to Mr. Ustalic. I have several copies where the signature of Mr. Ustalic appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at some point I am going to ask just for a five minute break just so I can talk with an interpreter, since I don't understand any Serbo-Croatian, but it should just be a five minute break, and I don't have many more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the document dated -- well, let me go then to the document dated the 16th of June, sir. That document says that the items are being dispatched for Celebici prison, and then it says "lunch and dinner." Does that mean that this material that you were picking up was supposed to be the lunch and the dinner of the Celebici -- for the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: Ma'am, you are right, this is what it was like, lunch and dinner, because at that time the kitchen in Igman was shelled and there was no electricity there, and I remember very well these pates, which were called Ding Dong, and they were given there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would you deliver them at once, the lunch and the dinner at the same time, or would you deliver them separately?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: This was an exceptional circumstance, ma'am. As I said, the kitchen was shelled and we could not approach the kitchen. There was no electricity or anything else. And this was an exceptional circumstance because the soldiers also received the same food, bread, pates, from the same receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, actually, let me ask you that also, with respect to that -- besides the food for the prisoners and for the personnel, the guards at Celebici, would you deliver food for anyone else in Celebici, besides the prisoners and the guards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And the weapons people, yes, Your Honour. I am asking whether or not there were significant numbers of soldiers who were in the Celebici barracks besides the guards, and if so, would you deliver food for them?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
utterances.text: The food was distributed, ma'am, to Celebici to the number of guards who were there. If there was a larger number, that that would be reported. And the barracks, ma'am, in Celebici, was called a school, and this was where another unit was placed before the prison this used to be a school and there was a unit there, which was also called the barracks. And the soldiers there would also receive the same food. This was a group from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And once the prison was established, would there -- were there significant numbers of soldiers who were in the Celebici barracks compound or had they left by the time it became a prison?

utterances.speaker: Zlatko Ustalic
